problemText: A friend tells you that a restaurant is located at 205 Main Street. What kind of location is this description?
choices: An absolute location, because a street address points to one exact building no matter who reads it
A relative location, because the restaurant is on Main Street instead of another street
An absolute location, because the restaurant has an exact position somewhere in the world
A relative location, because Main Street is the reference point being used
hints: Think about whether this description depends on already knowing where another place is.
Does this street address work the same way for everyone, or only for people who know Main Street?

problemText: Two students are trying to locate the same playground in their town. One student says it is "three blocks north of the library," and another student says it is "at 450 Oak Avenue." Which student's description would work for someone who has just moved to town and does not yet know where the library is?
choices: The first student, because giving a direction always helps someone find a place
The second student, because a street address does not depend on knowing another place first
Either student could help, because both descriptions point to the exact same spot
Neither student could help, because a playground cannot have both an absolute and relative location
hints: Ask yourself: could you find the playground using the first description if you had never heard of the library?
Does the second description require you to already know where another place is located?

problemText: A geographer is writing a field guide and needs to describe a mountain cabin. Which sentence is a relative location for the cabin?
choices: The cabin sits at 387 Forest Road, which is its exact street address and does not reference any other place
The cabin has one fixed position on Earth that stays the same regardless of how anyone describes it
The cabin is nestled in the pine trees two miles east of Miller Lake
The cabin belongs to a family that lives there year-round and is built from local materials
hints: Look for a description that mentions another place as a reference point.
Which choice gives both a distance and a direction from somewhere else?

problemText: A city library can be described as "next to the post office" or "across from the city park." Both descriptions are correct for the same library building. Explain what this tells you about the relationship between absolute location and relative location.
choices: The library must have two different absolute locations, one for each description
The post office and the city park must be located at the same spot, or the two descriptions would not both be correct
Relative locations are more accurate than absolute locations, so the library's true position must be the one that works for both descriptions
A single place has only one absolute location, but it can have many different relative locations depending on which reference point is chosen
hints: Think about how many fixed addresses a building can have versus how many different ways it can be described using nearby places.
If you change the reference point you use, what happens to the relative location description? What stays the same?

problemText: A student writes: "The baseball field is an absolute location because it is exactly halfway between the school and the community center." Identify the error in this reasoning and explain what kind of location this description actually is.
choices: The description is relative, because it names reference points (school and community center) and gives a distance relationship, so it depends on knowing where those places are
The description is actually absolute, because the word "exactly" indicates precision, and any precise measurement is independent of reference points and makes a location unique
The description is relative, because even though two known reference points are used, it depends on someone already understanding where both the school and the community center are located
The description is absolute only if both the school and the community center have their own street addresses that are written down and verified
hints: Does this description require you to already know where the school and community center are?
Does being very precise about a distance make a description independent of reference points, or does it still depend on them?

problemText: Three different people describe the location of the same museum using three different sentences: "The museum is at 92 Renaissance Avenue," "The museum is two blocks south of the train station," and "The museum is in the historic district downtown." Which statement correctly classifies all three descriptions and explains why they work the way they do?
choices: All three are absolute locations, because they all point to the exact same building even though the words are different

The first is absolute because it is an address, the second is relative because it uses the train station as a reference point, and the third is also relative because it depends on knowing what the historic district is
The first two are absolute and the third is relative, because street addresses and block distances are more exact measurements than region names
All three are relative locations, because none of them use latitude and longitude coordinates from a professional map
hints: For each description, ask: does it depend on already knowing where another place is, or does it work on its own?
Remember that a street address does not need any other place to point to the right spot, but a direction from another place does.

problemText: A mental map is the picture of a familiar place that a person carries in their head. Which of the following best describes what a mental map is built from?
choices: Something a person copies from a photograph or digital image they have seen on a computer or phone screen
A printed map that shows a place drawn to a fixed scale with a clear key and compass directions marked
A set of written or spoken directions that another person has explained or given to the student to memorize
The landmarks a person passes and the routes a person actually travels between them
hints: Think about how a person creates a mental map — do they copy it from somewhere, or do they build it themselves by moving through a space?
A mental map comes from a person's own experience of traveling through a place, not from something handed to them.

problemText: Maya walks the same route from her home to the bus stop every school day. She notices that the route passes the yellow mailbox, then the oak tree, and finally the corner store before she reaches the bus stop. One day, a visitor asks Maya to describe how to get from her home to the bus stop. Should Maya be concerned that her mental map is not drawn to a perfect scale?
choices: No, because Maya only needs the landmarks in the right order and the turns between them for someone to follow her route
Yes, because exact measurements are the only way a mental map can help someone reach their destination
Yes, because the distances on a mental map must match a ruler measurement or the directions will fail
No, because mental maps work best when they show only the most important landmarks regardless of true distance
hints: What is a mental map actually supposed to do — help someone measure exact distances, or help them find their way through a familiar space?
Think about whether the order and direction of landmarks matter more than the exact distance between them.

problemText: Two students walk into the school library from opposite ends of the building. One enters through the north door and the other through the south door. Both students visit the library regularly and have built mental maps of how to get around inside it. What should be true about their mental maps?
choices: Both mental maps must show the exact same landmarks in the exact same positions relative to each other and to the building
The mental maps could be different from each other, yet both could still work perfectly well
Only one mental map can be correct because the library building itself has only one true layout and arrangement of rooms
Both mental maps must be drawn to the same scale and measured the same way, or neither will be accurate for navigation
hints: Remember that a mental map is personal and built from one person's own trips through a space.
If two people start from different doors, they might pass different landmarks first, so their mental maps might look different — but could each one still guide that person through the library?

problemText: A student describes her mental map of walking from the classroom door to the water fountain like this: 'Out the door, past the lockers, turn left at the big window, then straight ahead to the fountain.' Another student says the description is wrong because he measured the distance with a tape measure and the actual hallway is longer than the student described. The first student says her mental map still works perfectly for finding the water fountain. Which student has the correct understanding of how mental maps are supposed to be evaluated?
choices: The second student is correct because mental maps must show the true measured distance between each landmark in order to be reliable
Neither student is correct because mental maps should be written down and checked against an official floor plan rather than described out loud
The first student is correct because a mental map works if the landmarks and turns are in the right order, not because distances are exact
The second student is correct because if distances are wrong, the person will become confused and get lost before reaching the destination
hints: Ask yourself: what is the real job of a mental map — to give exact measurements like a tape measure, or to help someone find their way?
Check whether the first student's description still names the landmarks in the right order with the right turns, even if distances are stretched.

problemText: An eighth-grader volunteers to help a younger student find the way from the school office to the gymnasium. The eighth-grader has walked to the office many times and can describe that route perfectly — 'past the main hallway, turn at the bulletin board, then to the office.' However, when asked to describe the path to the gymnasium, the eighth-grader says 'I don't know; I've never been there.' What does this show about what a mental map can and cannot do?
choices: Mental maps are not useful in schools because buildings contain too many different possible routes and hallways to remember clearly
Mental maps work only for frequently visited places like offices, not for places a student has passed by only a few times like gymnasiums
The eighth-grader should be able to describe the gymnasium route from memory even though she has never actually walked there herself
A mental map only covers space a person has actually moved through, and it cannot reach into a place the person has never visited
hints: Think about how a mental map is built — does it come from a person studying a printed map, or from moving through a space?
If someone has never walked to a place, what landmarks or turns could they possibly have stored in a mental map of that place?

problemText: A student describes her mental map of the walk from her bedroom to the kitchen by naming landmarks and turns in order: 'Out my door, past the bathroom, turn right at the stairs, down the hallway past the coat closet, turn left at the dining room table, then into the kitchen.' Later, she tries to describe the same walk backward, from the kitchen to the bedroom, reversing both the landmarks and the turns. Halfway through her backward description, she gets confused and says the route no longer makes sense. What does this tell you about her forward mental map?
choices: The forward mental map must contain a missing landmark or a missing turn that she forgot to name when describing the forward route
The forward mental map is correct but mental maps are designed only to work in one direction and cannot be reliably reversed or traced backward
The forward mental map proves that reversing any route is impossible because human brains process directions only in a forward order naturally
The forward mental map is flawed because she simply lacks the personal ability to think about directions in backward order or reverse sequence
hints: If a mental map truly connects all the landmarks and turns correctly, what should happen when you try to follow it in reverse order?
A route that only makes sense one way is missing something — what could that missing piece be?

problemText: A geographer is studying a small town nestled in a valley. She observes that the ground beneath the town is soft clay mixed with sand, and a river runs directly through the center of the town. Which of these two observations describes the site of this town?
choices: The river running through town, because water is always part of a site
The soft clay and sand ground, because it describes the exact spot the town sits on
Both the ground and the river equally, because they are both at this location
Neither one, because site only describes where the town is compared to other places
hints: Site focuses on what is true about the ground itself at this one patch of earth.
Think about whether the fact describes the spot itself or describes what surrounds the spot.

problemText: A town called Riverside sits on flat, well-drained ground with a strong freshwater spring at its center. The town is surrounded by dense forests in all directions, and the nearest other settlement is a three-week journey away on foot. Use the move-it test: if you picked up this exact patch of ground and moved it to a different location on Earth, which of these facts would travel with the ground and which would stay behind?
choices: All four facts would travel with the ground to its new location
The forests and distant neighbors would travel; the flat ground and spring would stay behind
The flat ground and the spring would travel; the forests and distant neighbors would stay behind
None of the four facts would travel; they are all determined by the surrounding region
hints: Ask yourself: if this patch of ground moved, would the properties of the ground itself move too, or only the neighboring features?
Ground properties like flatness and what resources lie in it are part of the spot itself.

problemText: Two students are debating why settlements form where they do. Student A claims: "A place needs a good situation — that is, it needs to be near other places or on a useful route." Student B claims: "A place needs a good site — that is, it needs ground that is solid, flat, and has fresh water nearby." Which student's claim correctly captures only one part of why settlements tend to grow in a location?
choices: Neither student is correct; settlements never consider location when forming
Only Student A is correct; situation is the only thing that determines settlement location
Only Student B is correct; site is the only thing that determines settlement location
Both Student A and Student B are correct; each describes one separate part that matters
hints: Remember: a settlement tends to grow where a useful site MEETS a useful situation, not where just one is good.
Think about whether site and situation are separate questions about a place, or whether one of them can tell you everything.

problemText: A researcher studies three invented locations. Location X has excellent flat, dry, solid ground with fresh water, but sits in the middle of a vast empty plain with no routes or other settlements nearby. Location Y has muddy, swampy ground that floods often, but sits directly where a major trade route crosses between two prosperous regions. Location Z has good flat ground with fresh water and also sits on a trade route between two regions. The researcher concludes: "Only Location Z will attract a growing settlement, because the other two are missing something." Evaluate this conclusion using what you know about site and situation.
choices: The conclusion is wrong because Location Y could attract a settlement if traders value the route enough, even though the ground is poor
The conclusion is correct because both site and situation must be good, and only Location Z has both
The conclusion is wrong because Location X has excellent site conditions that could support a self-sufficient settlement independent of trade connections and routes
The conclusion is correct because situation is always the dominant factor, making Location Y more attractive than Location Z despite its marshy, flood-prone ground
hints: Remember the mountain cabin example: a place can have an excellent site and a poor situation, or a poor site and an excellent situation, at the same time.
Think about whether traders or travelers might use a location for the route alone, even if the ground itself is difficult to build on.

problemText: A geographer examines why New York City grew so large. She notes four facts: (1) the harbor at the mouth of the Hudson River is deep and sheltered, protecting ships; (2) the Hudson River extends far inland into the continent; (3) the land around the harbor is mostly solid, rocky ground good for building; (4) the Atlantic Ocean opens from the harbor, offering routes to distant places across the sea. The geographer must explain which of these facts are about site, which are about situation, and how both kinds of facts work together to explain why a city grew there.
choices: Facts 2 and 4 describe the site because they identify the actual ground and water present at this location; facts 1 and 3 describe the situation because they name connections to distant places
Facts 1 and 3 describe the site; facts 2 and 4 describe the situation; the site provided solid, sheltered ground while the situation connected the harbor to inland and ocean routes
All four facts describe situation because they all involve water and routes that connect to places beyond this spot
Facts 1 and 2 describe the site by identifying the natural harbor and river present there; facts 3 and 4 describe the situation by showing how those features link to other regions and resources
hints: Separate the facts into two groups: those that describe the ground and water at this exact spot, and those that describe connections to places beyond it.
Use the move-it test: which facts would travel with the patch of ground if you moved it, and which facts depend on what happens to be nearby?

problemText: Two settlements, Alpha and Beta, face a puzzle about their own growth. Alpha sits on soft, marshy ground that floods seasonally, but it lies at the intersection of two major trade routes that connect four regions. Beta sits on high, dry, solid ground with a strong freshwater spring, but it is tucked into a remote mountain valley where no route passes nearby. Over the past century, Alpha has grown into a large, bustling city with many merchants and travelers, while Beta remains a small, quiet village. An observer claims: "This proves that situation always matters more than site, so any place with a good situation will grow large." Is this claim fully supported by the evidence, or is something missing from the reasoning?
choices: The claim is not fully supported because Beta's remote location proves that site quality is always more important than situation, so the observer's ranking is backwards
The claim is fully supported because Alpha's growth clearly shows that a good situation drives settlement growth regardless of site quality, making it the dominant factor everywhere

The claim is not fully supported because Alpha's poor site does require constant effort to build and maintain on marshy ground, and while its situation is excellent, we cannot conclude that situation always outweighs site in every location

The claim is fully supported because Beta's small size and poor access to trade routes demonstrate that even the best local site cannot support growth when situation isolates a settlement from economic opportunities
hints: Consider what the evidence really shows: Alpha grew large even with a poor site, but does this mean situation always wins, or does it mean that an excellent situation can overcome site problems in this case?
Think about whether one example can prove a rule that applies to all places, or whether it only shows what happened in these two specific situations.

problemText: Geography is the study of Earth's physical and human features and how they relate to each other. Which of the following is an example of a physical feature that geographers study?
choices: Trade routes, festivals, and schools
Cities, governments, and languages
Mountains, rivers, and climate
Farms, factories, and transportation networks
hints: Physical features are natural parts of Earth that exist whether or not people are present.
Look for something that is not built or organized by humans.

problemText: A geographer studies a desert region and notes several observations: the landscape has sand dunes covering most areas, rainfall occurs infrequently, people have constructed underground storage systems for water, and settlements are positioned near underground springs. Which observation describes a human feature rather than a physical feature?
choices: Sand dunes cover most of the land
Rainfall is very sparse
The few settlements are located near underground springs
People have built underground storage systems to hold water
hints: Ask yourself: would this exist if no people lived in the desert?
Human features are things people create or organize themselves.

problemText: Two towns, Riverside and Hillside, are both located in the same country and sit only 20 kilometers apart. Riverside sits in a flat valley where a river provides fresh water year-round, and it has grown into a busy port with boat traffic and many shops. Hillside sits on rocky, steep land with little water, and only a few hundred people live there in scattered homesteads. A geographer says these towns are different places. Which statement best explains what the geographer means?
choices: They have different mixes of physical and human features that make each one unique
They are far enough apart that they do not share any features with each other
They have different names, so they are separate places
One is a town and the other is a village, which makes them different types of places
hints: Place means the physical and human features that make one area different from every other area.
Look for an answer that mentions what is actually different about each location — its land, water, people, and the way people have built it up.

problemText: A student reads about a coastal fishing village that has developed strong traditions of boat-building and net-making passed down through families for hundreds of years. The student also learns that the village sits on a rocky coast with cold, fish-rich ocean currents nearby, and that the steep mountains behind the village make overland farming difficult. The student wants to explain why this village became known for fishing and boat-building rather than farming. Which two organizing ideas must the student combine to give a complete answer?
choices: Location and movement — the village is where it is, and fishing products move to other places
Human-environment interaction and place — the surroundings shaped what people chose to do, and this choice is part of what makes the village unique
Region and movement — the village is part of a region where fishing happens, and fish move to markets elsewhere
Place and location — the village's unique identity comes from its geography, and you can identify and find it on a map using its coordinates
hints: Think about what caused the village to specialize in fishing: was it the ocean currents and rocky coast (surroundings affecting people)?
Also think about what makes this village different from other villages — its traditions and skills are part of what makes it a unique place.

problemText: A geographer is preparing a lesson and creates a map that shades all the areas where coffee is grown as a major crop. On this map, the shaded areas include parts of Central America, South America, Africa, and Asia. These shaded areas are not connected to each other and do not form one continuous region on the map. The geographer labels the shaded areas on the map as "the world's coffee-growing region." Which organizing idea best describes what the geographer is showing by grouping these scattered areas together?
choices: Location, because each coffee-growing area occupies a specific latitude and longitude coordinate somewhere on Earth's surface
Movement, because coffee is produced in scattered places and transported across oceans and land routes to consumers worldwide
Region, because areas are grouped together because they share something in common even though they are not connected
Place, because each coffee-growing area has distinctive natural features and cultural practices that make it different from other agricultural zones
hints: A region does not have to be one solid piece of land — areas can be grouped by sharing a trait even if they are scattered far apart.
The key word in the definition is 'share something in common' — what do all these shaded areas have in common?

problemText: A geographer studies two different valleys. Valley A has rich soil, steady rainfall, and rivers that flow year-round, and it is home to intensive farms that feed a population of 50,000. Valley B has thin, rocky soil, very little rainfall, and rivers that dry up for months, yet people who live there have built terraced fields, water-collection systems, and canals to direct river water to crops, and it feeds a population of 30,000. The geographer says both valleys demonstrate human-environment interaction. Explain why each valley shows human-environment interaction, and identify what is different about how people interact with the surroundings in each case.
choices: Both valleys show human-environment interaction because in Valley A farms adapt to rich soil and steady water, and in Valley B farms also adapt to conditions, so the interaction is fundamentally the same process applied to different natural resources

Valley A demonstrates human-environment interaction because people chose to build farms to take advantage of good conditions, while Valley B demonstrates it because people were forced by harsh conditions to modify the landscape with terraces and canals, making them two separate types of interaction

Valley A shows human-environment interaction because it is located in a region with favorable geography, while Valley B shows human-environment interaction because it is located in a different region with unfavorable geography, so location differences explain why people interact differently

In Valley A, the environment shaped people's choice to farm because the soil and water are naturally good; in Valley B, people are also shaped by the environment but they have also changed the landscape by building systems to survive
hints: Human-environment interaction means the surroundings shape choices people make AND people can also change their surroundings — look for an answer that recognizes both directions.

In Valley A, favorable conditions shaped people's choice to farm. In Valley B, harsh conditions also shaped choices, but people went further and actually modified the landscape — both are human-environment interaction, but look different.
